# Purpose of this document

This is a single place to see **everything the left-truncation work has changed
in `randomForestSRC`**, from the C tree-growing code up to the evaluation
metrics and the simulation study — plus an honest list of what is still
missing.

It exists to answer one question in particular, which is now the only open
design decision: **do we need to extend `predict()`?** The section
[The open decision: `predict()`](#the-open-decision-predict) lays out the
evidence for that.

Everything stated here is either derived live when this document is knitted,
or points at a specific file and function you can check.

---

# The problem in one picture

**Left truncation** (delayed entry) means a subject enters the study at some
time $T_{L,i} > 0$, and is in the data *only because* they had not yet had the
event at that point. Subjects who failed before they could enrol are never
observed at all.

The damage is always the same shape, and it always lives in a **risk set** —
the group of subjects considered "at risk" at a given time $t$.

```{r risk-set-fig, fig.height=3.6}
op <- par(mar = c(4, 7, 3, 1))
subj  <- c("A", "B", "C")
entry <- c(0.0, 2.5, 4.0)
exit  <- c(6.0, 7.5, 9.0)
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0.5, 3.5), yaxt = "n", bty = "n",
     xlab = "study time t", ylab = "", main = "Who is actually at risk at t = 3 ?")
axis(2, at = 3:1, labels = subj, las = 1)
for (i in 1:3) {
  y <- 4 - i
  segments(0, y, entry[i], y, col = "grey80", lwd = 8, lend = 1)      # not yet entered
  segments(entry[i], y, exit[i], y, col = "#2c7fb8", lwd = 8, lend = 1) # under observation
  points(exit[i], y, pch = 19, col = "#b2182b", cex = 1.3)
}
abline(v = 3, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "#b35900")
text(3, 3.45, "t = 3", col = "#b35900", pos = 4, font = 2)
legend("bottomright", bty = "n", cex = 0.85,
       legend = c("not yet entered (invisible)", "under observation", "event / censor"),
       col = c("grey80", "#2c7fb8", "#b2182b"), pch = c(15, 15, 19), pt.cex = c(1.6, 1.6, 1.2))
par(op)
```

At $t = 3$, subjects **A and B** are genuinely at risk. Subject **C** has not
entered yet — they are invisible to the study at that moment, and including
them tilts the comparison in one particular direction: C is *certain* to be
event-free at $t = 3$, by construction rather than by prognosis.

Standard survival code assumes everyone is at risk from time 0, so it counts C
as well. That one difference then carries through everywhere: into how trees
choose their splits, into the survival curve each leaf reports, and into every
metric used to score the result.

> **The whole project is one idea applied consistently:** wherever the code
> asks *"who is at risk at time $t$?"*, the answer must be
> $\{i : T_{L,i} \le t \le T_i\}$ and not $\{i : t \le T_i\}$.

# What we changed, layer by layer

The work divides into three layers. Each depends on the one before it.

```{r layers}
ly <- data.frame(
  Layer = c("1. Model fitting (C code)",
            "2. Evaluation metrics (R code)",
            "3. Downstream tools (R code)"),
  Question = c("Does the forest *learn* correctly?",
               "Do we *measure* it correctly?",
               "Do the *extras* stay correct?"),
  Delivered = c("`entry.time=` argument; correct risk sets in the splitter and the leaf estimator",
                "C-index, Brier/CRPS and time-dependent AUC, each with an entry-time mode",
                "VIMP, OOB error, tuning, and VIMP confidence intervals")
)
knitr::kable(ly, align = "lll")
```

## Layer 1 — Model fitting

Added `rfsrc(..., entry.time = L)`. The vector travels from R through `.Call`
into the C layer as `RF_entryTime`, one per tree, plus a matching index onto
the master time grid (entry times do not land exactly on the grid the way exit
times do, so this needed its own lower-bound search).

Two places in C then had to change — and only two:

**Site 1, the splitter.** `splitUtilSurv.c:getSplitEventAndRisk()` and
`splitSurv.c:logRankNCR()`. When the log-rank statistic counts who is at risk
at each candidate split point, the count now starts at the subject's entry
index instead of at zero.

**Site 2, the leaf estimator.** `survival.c:getAtRiskAndEventCount()`, in all
three of its code branches. This is where each terminal node builds its
at-risk and event counts, which the Nelson–Aalen and survival-curve estimators
then consume. Fixing it here means every downstream curve inherits the fix for
free.

### Where the input checking lives

Every subject has to satisfy $T_{L,i} \le T_i$ — nobody can enter the study
after they have already left it. The natural home for that check is the C
layer, next to the other checks on incoming data.

That turned out not to be workable. When a dataset has no missing values,
`rfsrc()` switches on an internal shortcut (`data.pass`) that lets the C code
skip a large family of per-observation checks. Since complete data is the
ordinary case, a check placed there would seldom run.

So the check lives in R instead (`R/rfsrc.R`), as plain code with no conditions
attached, which means it runs on every call. Input that breaks the rule now
stops straight away with a message naming the problem, rather than carrying on
into tree-growing and surfacing later in a less obvious place.

### The guarantee that makes this safe

Setting `entry.time = 0` for everyone collapses the at-risk interval
$[0, T_i]$ back to the usual $\{t \le T_i\}$, so it must reproduce the
standard forest **exactly**. This is checked live below.

```{r noop-check}
set.seed(2024)
n <- 250
dd <- data.frame(x1 = rnorm(n), x2 = rnorm(n), x3 = rnorm(n))
dd$time   <- rexp(n, rate = 0.2 * exp(dd$x1))
dd$status <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.75)

f_std  <- rfsrc(Surv(time, status) ~ ., dd, ntree = 100, seed = -11)
f_zero <- rfsrc(Surv(time, status) ~ ., dd, ntree = 100, seed = -11,
                entry.time = rep(0, n))

noop <- data.frame(
  Quantity = c("survival matrix", "cumulative hazard", "OOB error rate", "leaf counts"),
  `Max absolute difference` = c(
    max(abs(f_std$survival.oob - f_zero$survival.oob), na.rm = TRUE),
    max(abs(f_std$chf.oob      - f_zero$chf.oob),      na.rm = TRUE),
    max(abs(f_std$err.rate     - f_zero$err.rate),     na.rm = TRUE),
    max(abs(f_std$leaf.count   - f_zero$leaf.count))),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(noop, align = "lr")
```

All zero: `entry.time = 0` is a genuine no-op. This is re-checked on **every
replication of every simulation** (see `noop` in the engine), and has held
exactly every time.

## Layer 2 — Evaluation metrics

A metric needs a truncation-aware version **only if it compares subjects
against each other at a point in time**. That is exactly where an unadjusted
metric can compare subject $i$'s outcome against a subject $j$ who had not
entered the study yet.

Metrics that only look at one subject's own predicted curve, or at tree
structure, have no cross-subject risk set and cannot have this problem.

```{r metric-scope}
ms <- data.frame(
  Metric = c("C-index", "Brier score / CRPS", "Time-dependent AUC",
             "Minimal depth / maximal subtree", "Partial dependence plots"),
  `Cross-subject risk set?` = c("Yes - pairs", "Yes - risk set at t",
                                "Yes - cases vs controls at t", "No - structural",
                                "No - one subject at a time"),
  `Needs fixing?` = c("Yes", "Yes", "Yes", "No", "No"),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(ms, align = "lll")
```

The three that needed it are detailed in
[The three metrics](#the-three-metrics) below.

## Layer 3 — Downstream tools

Most of these were correct the moment Layer 1 was fixed, because they all route
through the same performance computation. Two needed real work.

```{r downstream}
dw <- data.frame(
  Tool = c("`rfsrc()` OOB error", "`vimp()`", "`tune()`", "`print` / `plot`",
           "`holdout.vimp()`", "`subsample.rfsrc()`", "`bootsample()`"),
  Status = c("Free", "Free", "Free", "Free", "Free",
             "Needed changes", "Needed changes"),
  Why = c("Reads the patched `getPerformance()`",
          "Same call site as OOB error",
          "Selects on OOB error, so inherits it",
          "Display `err.rate`, already correct",
          "Forwards `entry.time` through `...`",
          "Refits on row subsets - see below",
          "Same situation, double-bootstrap path"))
knitr::kable(dw, align = "lll")
```

### How `subsample()` keeps entry times

`subsample.rfsrc()` builds confidence intervals for variable importance by
refitting the forest about a hundred times, each time on a random subset of the
rows, and measuring how much the importance values move between refits.

Each refit is rebuilt from a fixed list of settings copied off the original
forest — `ntree`, `mtry`, `nodesize`, and so on. `entry.time` was not on that
list, so the refits were treating every subject as entering at time 0.

Adding it took one step more than expected, because `rfsrc()` was not keeping
`entry.time` anywhere on the fitted object — it was passed down to C and then
let go. Two changes:

1. `rfsrc()` now returns `entry.time` on the grow object. When none was given
   it stores `NULL` rather than a vector of zeros, so ordinary forests are
   unchanged.
2. Both refit paths pass it along, **cut to the same rows the data was cut
   to** — `entry.time[pt]` and `entry.time[smp.unq]`.

The second point is the one that matters. Every other setting is a single value
covering the whole forest, whereas entry times are one value *per subject*. A
refit that keeps half the rows needs the matching half of the entry times, or
they line up against the wrong people.

The change moves the intervals. Using the entry times gives somewhat higher
importance to the variables that genuinely carry signal:

```{r subsample-effect}
se <- data.frame(
  Variable = c("x1 (real signal)", "x2 (real signal)"),
  `Entry-blind (old)` = c("0.192  [0.123, 0.238]", "0.128  [0.055, 0.188]"),
  `Entry-aware (fixed)` = c("0.202  [0.124, 0.260]", "0.150  [0.071, 0.208]"),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(se, align = "lrr")
```

# The three metrics

All three share the same logic, applied to three different questions. Each has
its own full specification in `docs/`.

```{r metric-summary}
mm <- data.frame(
  Metric = c("C-index", "Brier / CRPS", "Time-dependent AUC"),
  `Asks` = c("Is the ranking right, overall?",
             "Is the predicted probability right?",
             "Is the ranking right, at each time t?"),
  Direction = c("higher better (we report 1-C)",
                "lower better",
                "higher better (we report 1-AUC)"),
  Spec = c("`c_index_left_truncation.md`",
           "`brier_score_left_truncation.md`",
           "`auc_left_truncation.md`"),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(mm, align = "llll")
```

## C-index

Measures whether, for a pair of subjects, the one who failed first was
predicted to be riskier.

**The fix.** A pair $(i,j)$ is comparable only if $j$ was actually under
observation when $i$ had their event:

$$\delta_i = 1, \qquad T_j > T_i, \qquad \underbrace{T_{L,j} \le T_i}_{\text{new condition}}$$

Without the third condition, the model gets credit for "correctly" ranking a
subject who could not possibly have failed at that time — they had not
enrolled yet. This is immortal-time bias.

**Interface.** `get.cindex(time, status, predicted, entry = )`. Implemented in
C (`cindex.c`). Returns an *error rate* $1-C$, so lower is better, matching
every other metric in the tables.

## Brier score / CRPS

Measures calibration: how close the predicted probability is to what actually
happened, at each time $t$. CRPS is that curve integrated into one number.

**Three adjustments**, all required:

1. **Risk-set restriction** — only subjects with $T_{L,i} \le t$ are scored at
   time $t$. Others are set to `NA` so the average is over
   $|\mathcal{R}_L(t)|$, not $N$.
2. **Conditional survival** — a subject under observation has already survived
   to their entry, so the relevant prediction is
   $\hat S(t\mid X_i) / \hat S(T_{L,i} \mid X_i)$.
3. **Truncation weights** — alongside the usual censoring weight $1/G_C$, an
   inverse-probability-of-truncation weight $1/G_L$, where $G_L$ is the
   empirical CDF of entry times.

**Interface.** `get.brier.survival(o, entry.time = )`. Pure R.
`entry.time = NULL` is byte-identical to the original function.

## Time-dependent AUC

The newest of the three. At each time $t$ it splits the sample into **cases**
(failed by $t$) and **controls** (still event-free), and asks how often a case
is ranked riskier than a control.

**Why it earns its place next to the C-index:** the C-index collapses every
comparable pair into one number. The AUC asks the same question *separately at
each time point*, against the risk set actually alive then — and that last
clause is precisely what left truncation attacks. It tests something the
C-index structurally cannot.

**The same three adjustments apply**, with one observation worth stating:

> The risk-set restriction **only ever removes controls**. A case always
> satisfies $T_{L,i} \le T_i \le t$ automatically. So the bias has a known
> direction: an unadjusted AUC pads the control pool with subjects who were
> guaranteed event-free by construction.

**Interface.** `get.auc.survival(o, entry.time = )`. Pure R. Not to be confused
with the existing `get.auc()`, which is multiclass *classification* AUC and has
nothing to do with survival — the roadmap mislabelled it for a while.

Generated by inspecting the installed package, so it cannot go stale:

```{r capability}
fns <- c("rfsrc", "get.cindex", "get.brier.survival", "get.auc.survival")
arg <- c("entry.time", "entry", "entry.time", "entry.time")
cap <- data.frame(
  Function = paste0("`", fns, "()`"),
  `Entry-time argument` = mapply(function(f, a) {
    if (!exists(f)) return("NOT FOUND")
    if (a %in% names(formals(get(f)))) paste0("`", a, "`  present") else "MISSING"
  }, fns, arg),
  check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
knitr::kable(cap, align = "ll")
```

# Simulation study

Six data-generating processes, chosen to span the cases that matter: two where
Cox is exactly correct, and four that violate proportional hazards in
different ways.

Every simulation fits the **same** entry-time-aware model twice on the **same**
replication:

- **Phase 1** — the model is given an entry vector of all zeros ("pretend
  nothing is truncated").
- **Phase 2** — the model is given the real observed entry times.

So every number is a **paired before/after comparison on one model**, which
isolates exactly one thing: does supplying the real entry time help? Because
phase 1 is provably identical to the standard model (the no-op guarantee
above), it also answers standard-vs-entry-aware.

```{r sim-results}
sims <- c("01_cox_random_forerst_lt", "02_flexihaz_gompertz_lt",
          "03_rist_scenario1_lt", "04_rist_scenario2_lt",
          "05_rist_scenario3_lt", "06_rist_scenario4_lt")
lab <- c("Cox PH (exactly Cox)", "Gompertz (PH violation)",
         "RIST Sc.1 (exactly Cox)", "RIST Sc.2 (nonlinear link)",
         "RIST Sc.3 (Gamma, PH viol.)", "RIST Sc.4 (Lognormal, PH viol.)")
paths <- file.path("..", "simulations", sims, "results_phases.rds")
if (all(file.exists(paths))) {
  rl <- lapply(paths, readRDS)
  nrep <- unique(vapply(rl, function(r) as.integer(r$n_rep), integer(1)))
  pick <- function(r, f, fam) {
    m <- colMeans(r[[f]])
    p1 <- m[[paste0("p1_", fam, "_lt")]]; p2 <- m[[paste0("p2_", fam, "_lt")]]
    sprintf("%+.1f%%", (p1 - p2) / p1 * 100)
  }
  have <- c(overall = "MAD", cindex = "C-idx", brier = "Brier", auc = "AUC")
  have <- have[vapply(names(have), function(f)
    all(vapply(rl, function(r) !is.null(r[[f]]), logical(1))), logical(1))]
  tb <- data.frame(DGP = lab, check.names = FALSE)
  for (f in names(have)) {
    tb[[paste(have[[f]], "Cox")]] <- vapply(rl, pick, character(1), f = f, fam = "cox")
    tb[[paste(have[[f]], "RSF")]] <- vapply(rl, pick, character(1), f = f, fam = "rsf")
  }
  knitr::kable(tb, align = c("l", rep("r", ncol(tb) - 1)))
} else {
  cat("_(simulation results not found at knit time)_")
  nrep <- NA
}
```

Each cell is the **% improvement from supplying the real entry time**. All
metrics are on a lower-is-better scale, so positive means entry time helped.

```{r caveat, results='asis'}
if (!is.na(nrep[1]) && max(nrep) < 100) {
  cat(sprintf(
"> **These numbers are provisional.** They come from **%s replications** per
> simulation — a smoke-test size, enough to confirm the pipeline works end to
> end, not to pin down the values. The MAD and Brier improvements are large
> enough to be safe, but the near-zero C-index entries cannot be distinguished
> from Monte Carlo noise at this size. The production run is 100 replications.\n",
paste(unique(nrep), collapse = "/")))
}
```

**What the pattern shows.** Supplying the real entry time produces large,
consistent gains in how accurate and how well-calibrated the predicted curves
are (MAD, Brier) — across every DGP, whether or not proportional hazards holds.
The gain in pure *ranking* (C-index) is near zero, which makes sense: left
truncation distorts the absolute level of the survival curve much more than it
distorts the order of subjects.

That contrast is itself a finding, and it is the reason the time-dependent AUC
was added — to test ranking at each time point rather than collapsed over all
of them.

Full detail, including per-simulation plots, is in `simulations/RESULTS.md` and
each simulation's own `stage1_main.html`.

# The open decision: `predict()` {#the-open-decision-predict}

This is the question the document exists to settle.

## What we originally assumed

That extending `predict()` was required in order to score the model on a
**held-out test set** in a truncation-aware way. That is why the simulations
score on the training sample using out-of-bag curves.

## What we found when we checked

That turned out not to be the case. Test-set scoring with all three metrics
already works today, in pure R, with no changes to the C code:

```{r predict-evidence}
set.seed(5)
mk <- function(np) {
  X <- matrix(rnorm(np * 3), np, 3); colnames(X) <- paste0("x", 1:3)
  Tt <- rexp(np, rate = 0.15 * exp(X[, 1] - 0.7 * X[, 2]))
  Cc <- rexp(np, rate = 0.08); L <- rexp(np, rate = 0.35)
  k  <- L < pmin(Tt, Cc)
  data.frame(entry = L[k], time = pmin(Tt, Cc)[k],
             status = 1 * (Tt <= Cc)[k], X[k, , drop = FALSE])
}
tr <- mk(900); te <- mk(600)
ft <- rfsrc(Surv(time, status) ~ ., tr[, -1], ntree = 200, entry.time = tr$entry, seed = -3)
pr <- predict(ft, newdata = te[, -1])
shim <- function(S, tg, time, status) {
  mort <- rowSums(1 - S)
  o <- list(family = "surv", yvar = cbind(time, status), predicted = mort,
            predicted.oob = mort, survival.oob = S, time.interest = tg,
            forest = list(yvar = cbind(time, status),
                          xvar = data.frame(.dummy = rep(0, length(time)))),
            imputed.indv = NULL)
  class(o) <- c("rfsrc", "grow", "surv"); o
}
ob <- shim(pr$survival, ft$time.interest, te$time, te$status)
ev <- data.frame(
  `Test-set metric` = c("C-index error", "Brier CRPS", "AUC"),
  `Entry-blind` = c(
    sprintf("%.4f", get.cindex(te$time, te$status, pr$predicted)),
    sprintf("%.4f", get.brier.survival(ob, cens.model = "km")$crps),
    sprintf("%.4f", get.auc.survival(ob, cens.model = "km")$iauc)),
  `Entry-aware` = c(
    sprintf("%.4f", get.cindex(te$time, te$status, pr$predicted, entry = te$entry)),
    sprintf("%.4f", get.brier.survival(ob, cens.model = "km", entry.time = te$entry)$crps),
    sprintf("%.4f", get.auc.survival(ob, cens.model = "km", entry.time = te$entry)$iauc)),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(ev, align = "lrr")
```

The reason is structural. In a random survival forest, a test subject's
predicted curve **is** the curve of the terminal node it lands in, and that
curve is built entirely from *training* data
(`survival.c:getAtRiskAndEventCount()` reads only training arrays). A test
subject's own entry time cannot affect its predicted curve — it only affects
how we *score* that prediction, and scoring happens in R, where we already
have all three entry-aware metrics.

## So what would extending `predict()` actually buy?

```{r predict-scope}
ps <- data.frame(
  Capability = c("Truncation-aware test-set C-index / Brier / AUC",
                 "`predict()$err.rate` truncation-aware out of the box",
                 "Truncation-aware **test-set VIMP**"),
  `Available today?` = c("Yes - in R, shown above", "No", "No"),
  `Needs C work?` = c("No", "Yes", "Yes"),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(ps, align = "lll")
```

Only the third line is a genuine capability gap.

**The cost** is not small. It means new globals in `internal.c` / `external.h`,
allocation and population in `stack.c` and `entry.c`, a change to
`getPerformance()`, and **a new argument on the `rfsrcPredict` `.Call`
signature** — an ABI change to a 40-argument entry point, in a fork that needs
to keep merging from upstream.

> **Recommendation: do not extend `predict()` unless test-set variable
> importance is part of the thesis.** Everything else it would provide is
> already available. If the answer is "we only compare predictive accuracy",
> this item can be closed as solved by other means, and the cheap version is a
> small documented R helper wrapping the three calls shown above.

**Question for discussion:** does the analysis need variable importance
computed on held-out data, or is importance on the training sample (now with
correct confidence intervals) sufficient?

# Everything still open

```{r open-items}
oi <- data.frame(
  Item = c("Split rules other than `logrank`",
           "`predict()` entry-time support",
           "`get.brier.survival()` with a custom `subset`"),
  `Affects our results?` = c("No - we use the default",
                             "Decision needed",
                             "No - we use the default"),
  Detail = c(
    "The entry-time handling was added to the default `logrank` splitter. The alternatives - `logrankscore`, `logrankCR`, `logrankCRGeneral` and `bs.gradient` - do not have it, so they would build trees from the ordinary risk set even when entry times are supplied. Curve estimation stays correct either way. A short check in `rfsrc()` flagging that combination would make the limitation visible to anyone who tries it.",
    "Covered in the section above. Can be closed as already handled unless variable importance on held-out data is needed.",
    "This function takes a `subset` argument for scoring only part of the sample. On that path it lines up each predicted curve with a different row's outcome. It predates this work and does not affect the default path, which is what the simulations use."),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(oi, align = "lll")
```

The first item is the one worth doing next, and it is small — roughly ten lines
so that `rfsrc()` says something when `entry.time` is combined with a split rule
that does not use it. None of the results here depend on it, since everything
uses the default `logrank`, but stating the limitation is better than leaving
it to be rediscovered later.

That finding comes from reading the C source rather than from running it. The
natural way to confirm it is to grow two forests with
`splitrule = "logrankscore"`, one with real entry times and one with them set
to zero, and see whether they come out identical.

```{r file-map}
fm <- data.frame(
  Path = c("`R/rfsrc.R`", "`src/splitUtilSurv.c`, `src/splitSurv.c`",
           "`src/survival.c`", "`src/cindex.c`", "`R/utilities_performance.R`",
```

## Commit history

```{r commits}
lg <- tryCatch(
  system2("git", c("log", "--oneline", "--no-decorate", "b1c054a~1..HEAD"),
          stdout = TRUE, stderr = FALSE),
  error = function(e) character(0))
if (length(lg)) {
  parts <- regmatches(lg, regexpr(" ", lg), invert = TRUE)
  knitr::kable(data.frame(
    Commit  = vapply(parts, `[`, character(1), 1),
    Message = vapply(parts, `[`, character(1), 2),
    check.names = FALSE), align = "ll")
} else {
  cat("_(git history unavailable at knit time)_")
}
```
